position: Chapter presents both sides: contributors who want to keep a purely economic consumer welfare focus and those open to broader factors; the author's recommendations are stated as principles on which contributors agreed or dissented.
proposal: The chapter says the consumer welfare standard should guide FTC action but be expanded beyond price in appropriate cases with strong evidence, and calls the FTC's rescission of its 2015 Section 5 policy statement ill-considered. It describes a split among conservatives over whether Big Tech warrants a more proactive approach, urges better measurement of consumer surplus and openness to behavioral explanations of market power, and recommends a chairman's office role for state attorney general cooperation.

status_summary: The FTC's continued enforcement is not counted here as a change: it kept the 2023 Merger Guidelines in effect on 2025-02-18, appealed its loss in FTC v. Meta (district court ruling November 2025; notice of appeal filed 2026-01-26 and FTC opening brief filed 2026-05-22 in the D.C. Circuit, with no decision), continues its separate antitrust case against Amazon (trial set for 2027-03-29 per trade press), and on 2026-08-31 joined 22 states in suing Amazon over an advertising auction, a case coverage frames as deception. What is counted is the FTC's use of harms other than price in specific matters. In the Omnicom and Interpublic merger, announced 2025-06-23 and finalized with changes on 2025-09-26, the FTC described the concern as coordination among advertising agencies to steer spending away from publishers on political or ideological grounds, which it said could reduce publishers' content and investment and distort public discussion, and the order bars such coordination. A 2026-02-06 merger consent analysis (Sevita and BrightSpring) says harm would show up in quality and choice because state Medicaid agencies set prices, and on 2026-04-15 the FTC and eight state attorneys general filed a Sherman Act and Section 5 complaint against three advertising holding companies with stipulated orders that bar agreements to restrict dealing on political or ideological grounds. The Chairman's remarks of 2025-05-07 name quality, innovation, labor and speech among the harms of abused economic power but do not mention the consumer welfare standard, and a law-firm summary of his 2026-04-15 Senate testimony says he stressed enforcing within the statute's limits. No policy statement, rule or speech was found that announces a change in the consumer welfare standard, and the chapter's other steps were not found: the FTC's policy statements page lists no Section 5 unfair-methods statement after the 2022 statement (a business group's analysis of 2026-04-02 says that statement remains in effect), and no work on consumer surplus measurement or behavioral explanations of market power or designated state attorney general role in the chairman's office was found.

timeline.event: FTC Chairman Ferguson announces that the 2023 Merger Guidelines remain in effect as the framework for FTC merger review, citing the value of stability; a law-firm summary adds that DOJ issued a parallel instruction and that both agencies left open later revision. This is continuity with the prior framework, not a change.

The FTC opens a public inquiry and issues a request for information (comments due 2025-05-21) on how technology platforms deny or degrade users' access based on speech or affiliations, asking about potentially unfair or deceptive practices and about potentially unfair methods of competition, including whether such conduct may stem from a lack of competition. No resulting report or enforcement action was found.

In remarks to the International Competition Network conference in Edinburgh, Chairman Ferguson says antitrust law protects consumers and workers from concrete harms of abused economic power, naming degraded quality, threats to innovation, lower wages and platform censorship of political speech, and favors acting after specific harmful conduct is shown; the remarks do not mention the consumer welfare standard, Section 5 or the merger guidelines.

The FTC announces a proposed consent order in Omnicom's acquisition of Interpublic (vote 2-0-1, Commissioner Meador recused). The release describes the concern as coordination among advertising agencies, including through industry associations, to avoid certain websites, which it says could cut publishers' ad revenue, content and investment and distort public discussion, and the order bars coordination to steer advertising on political or ideological grounds. The FTC finalized the order with changes and a compliance monitor on 2025-09-26.

The FTC files its notice of appeal to the D.C. Circuit from the November 2025 ruling for Meta in FTC v. Meta (D.D.C. No. 1:20-cv-03590, Judge Boasberg, who found the FTC did not prove monopoly power because the relevant market includes TikTok and YouTube); the appeal is docketed as No. 26-5028. An FTC spokesperson had confirmed the plan to appeal on 2026-01-20 (Bloomberg; MediaNama report of 2026-01-21).

FTC publishes a proposed consent order requiring divestitures in Sevita's acquisition of assets from BrightSpring (91 FR 5477); the analysis applies the 2023 Merger Guidelines' structural presumption (HHI change above 100, combined share above 30 percent) and says the main harms are to quality and choice because state Medicaid agencies set prices.

The FTC and eight state attorneys general (Florida, Indiana, Iowa, Montana, Nebraska, Texas, Utah, West Virginia) file a complaint in the Northern District of Texas against WPP, Publicis and Dentsu, charging under Section 1 of the Sherman Act and Section 5 of the FTC Act that they agreed on common 'brand safety' standards through trade groups; stipulated orders entered the same day, without admission of liability, bar agreements to restrict dealing with publishers on political, ideological or similar grounds and impose a five-year monitorship.

The FTC files its opening brief in its D.C. Circuit appeal in FTC v. Meta (No. 26-5028; notice of appeal filed 2026-01-26); the clerk set Meta's brief for 2026-08-20 and final briefs for 2026-10-20, and no argument date was listed.

title: Extend consumer welfare beyond price in some cases and weigh a more active Big Tech stance
uncertainties: Stage decision (in_progress kept at 30; proposed considered). Basis: continued enforcement is not a change and is not counted (retained Merger Guidelines, the Meta appeal, the Amazon cases, and the 2026-08-31 Amazon advertising suit, which coverage frames as deception). No FTC policy statement, rule or speech was found that adopts or announces a change in the consumer welfare standard (searches in this pass on a 2026 Section 5 statement, on Ferguson and Meador speeches about the consumer welfare standard and non-price harms, and a read of the FTC policy statements page, which lists no new Section 5 statement; the 2026-09-09 rescission on that page concerns a 2021 health-app statement). The stage rests instead on two operative FTC orders and one complaint in which the FTC itself states a non-price theory of harm: Omnicom and Interpublic (public discussion, publisher content and investment; final order 2025-09-26), Sevita and BrightSpring (quality and choice; proposed order published 2026-02-06, final approval not checked) and the 2026-04-15 advertising holding company case (stipulated orders, no admission of liability). These are consent outcomes and a complaint, not adjudicated findings, so the chapter's 'strong evidence' condition has not been tested, and they fit the chapter's free-speech and democratic-institution examples more than its price-versus-quality examples. If only policy statements, rules or announced standards counted, the stage would be proposed at most (the 2025-02-20 request for information and the Chairman's 2025-05-07 remarks), and a reader could reasonably choose that. Evidence limits: the 2022 Section 5 statement's continued effect rests on a business group's 2026-04-02 analysis and on its absence of a rescission on the FTC's policy statements page (the page summary could not be matched to every entry); the Omnicom decision and order copy read has a blank docket number and issuance date; the Chairman's 2026-04-15 testimony is known only through a law-firm summary; the exact date of the Meta ruling is not given in the sources read (November 2025), and the Bloomberg article was seen only as a search result, though the MediaNama report of 2026-01-21 confirms the appeal; the FTC's D.C. Circuit brief (2026-05-22) is now confirmed on the docket copy, but no argument date was found; the Amazon advertising suit is described through one States Newsroom article that does not name the statutes invoked; the trial date of the separate FTC v. Amazon antitrust case (2027-03-29) comes from trade press of October 2026 (MLex, PYMNTS), which supersedes the February 2027 date in an MLex summary of 2025-06-04. The 2025-02-20 request for information has no follow-up report in the searches run. The FTC's proposed enforcement policy statement on personalized pricing (listed on the policy statements page, dated 2026-08-19) is a consumer protection matter and was not treated as progress here. Trump v. Slaughter (decided 2026-06-29) concerns FTC commissioners' removal and was not analyzed for this item. Commentary from Reason (2025-05-22) characterizes the February 2025 Joint Labor Task Force as a departure from the consumer welfare standard; that is a commentator's characterization of a labor-market initiative, and it was not counted. Checked on 2026-10-08: The FTC's page of policy statements, as read on this date, lists no policy statement on Section 5 unfair methods of competition after the one of 2022-11-10 and no rescission of it (2026 entries concern age verification, AI accuracy, disparate impact and personalized pricing, and a 2026-09-09 rescission of a 2021 health-app statement); a U.S. Chamber of Commerce analysis of 2026-04-02 says the 2022 statement remains in effect and reports no FTC plan for Section 5 guidance (ftc.gov) Update 2026-10-16: the FTC policy statements page lists no Section 5 competition statement after 2022-11-10 and no consumer welfare statement; entries after 2026-04-15 concern AI accuracy (2026-07-01), disparate impact (2026-08-07), personalized pricing (2026-08-19) and a rescission (2026-09-09), none counted. The Amazon trial date of 2027-03-29 and the 2026-10-09 denial rest on trade press (MLex, PYMNTS); the court docket was not read. The Meta docket was read as retrieved on 2026-06-02, so later filings and any argument date are unknown. The Google search and ad tech cases are Department of Justice matters, not FTC, and were not counted; a news report states the ad tech remedies decision (unsealed 2026-09-16) ordered behavioral remedies and no divestiture, and the search remedies ruling of September 2025 and the Meta ruling were not re-read this pass. No FTC or DOJ policy statement on the consumer welfare standard after 2026-04-15 was found. Independent review 2026-10-16: the D.C. Circuit docket copy (Justia, retrieved 2026-06-02) confirms the notice of appeal of 2026-01-26, the FTC brief of 2026-05-22 and the clerk's schedule (Meta brief 2026-08-20, reply 2026-09-29, final briefs 2026-10-20); filings after 2026-06-02 are not shown. A PYMNTS report of 2026-10-11 states that Judge John Chun (W.D. Wash.) on 2026-10-09 denied Amazon's request to move the FTC v. Amazon trial from 2027-03-29 to June 2027; the court record was not read, and as a trial-scheduling ruling it is recorded here rather than in the timeline or court status.
